successor: Early Qing (Manchu Qing dynasty), after a six-week occupation of Beijing by Li Zicheng's Shun regime
source2: Kenneth M. Swope, The Military Collapse of China's Ming Dynasty, 1618-44, Routledge 2014 (Google Books) - https://books.google.com/books?id=WRaoAgAAQBAJ
notes: Internal rebel Li Zicheng took Beijing April 1644 and Chongzhen hanged himself; within weeks Manchu-led forces (based outside the core) with Wu Sangui drove Li out and occupied Beijing. Priority rule gives T2; widespread rebellions give Q4=Y.

successor: Carolingian Empire II (Lothar I as emperor; partition at Verdun 843)
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Treaty of Verdun' and 'Louis I: Rebellion and recovery' - https://www.britannica.com/event/Treaty-of-Verdun ; https://www.britannica.com/biography/Louis-I-Holy-Roman-emperor/Rebellion-and-recovery
notes: 840 is Louis the Pious's death; dynasty and imperial office continued under Lothar I, who kept the Middle Realm with Aachen after Verdun (843). Sons' revolts (830, 833) and the brothers' war 840-843 give Q4=Y. Database period split.

successor: No successor state in the core: Early Iron Age squatter farming communities at Hattusa; Hittite royal line continued at Carchemish (Neo-Hittite kingdoms) outside the core
source1: Juergen Seeher, 'After the Empire: Observations on the Early Iron Age in Central Anatolia', in I. Singer (ed.), Ipamati kistamati pari tumatimis, Tel Aviv University 2010 - https://www.academia.edu/16780675
source2: Trevor Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites, Oxford University Press (new ed. 2005), preface and introduction - https://www.academia.edu/11566287/TheKingdomOfTheHittites
notes: Seeher: Hattusa was 'given up rather than being conquered'; court and priesthood left, official buildings burned later, no battle horizon; squatter farmers followed. Older views blame Kaska or Phrygians. Q4 rests on Tarhuntassa rivalry and grain shortages.

successor: Roman Republic (Pompey); Hyrcanus II kept as high priest without royal title under Roman Syria
notes: Civil war between Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II (67-63 BCE); Pompey intervened, took Jerusalem in 63 BCE, subjected Judaea to Rome and removed the royal title. Brief Hasmonean restoration under Antigonus 40-37 BCE did not undo this.

successor: Papal States under Innocent III (Papal States - High Medieval Period)
source1: Catholic Encyclopedia (1912), 'States of the Church', New Advent - https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14257a.htm
notes: 1198 is Innocent III's election: he exacted oaths from Rome's senators and prefect and recovered provinces, restoring rather than replacing papal rule; papal sovereignty runs 756-1870. Q4: Roman commune and senate, Arnold of Brescia, 1159-77 schism, imperial pressure.

Henry III's death (1589) ended the Valois line; the recognised heir Henry of Navarre succeeded as first Bourbon king within the same monarchy. Wars of Religion give Q4=Y; Catholic League held Paris until Henry IV entered in 1594.

successor: British Empire (Protectorate of Northern Nigeria; client sultan Attahiru II installed)
notes: British-led forces under Lugard took Kano (Feb 1903) and Sokoto (Mar 1903); caliph Attahiru I fled and was killed at Burmi (Jul 1903); caliphate abolished, sultan kept as client title. Database 1904 slightly late. Q4: internal decay, emirate conflicts.

successor: None for c. 150-200 years (Hazor abandoned); small Iron I village settlement later
source1: Amnon Ben-Tor, 'Who Destroyed Canaanite Hazor?', Biblical Archaeology Review 2013 - https://www.academia.edu/35948616/Who_Destroyed_Canaanite_Hazor
source2: Noah Wiener, 'Scorched Wheat May Provide Answers on the Destruction of Canaanite Tel Hazor' (quoting Sharon Zuckerman), Biblical Archaeology Society 2012 - https://www.biblicalarchaeology.org/daily/news/scorched-wheat-may-provide-answers-on-the-destruction-of-canaanite-tel-hazor/
notes: Hazor was violently burned in the 13th century BCE, then abandoned. Agent disputed: Ben-Tor argues external conquest, Zuckerman an internal revolt, so T2 and T1 cannot be separated. Database 1175 BCE too late; destruction no earlier than c.1250.

successor: Kidinuid kings of Susa and Anshan (c. 1500-1400 BCE); link to sukkalmahs unknown
source1: Francois Vallat, 'Elam i. The History of Elam', Encyclopaedia Iranica - https://www.iranicaonline.org/articles/elam-i
notes: Last sukkalmahs (Tan-Uli, Kuk-Nashur III) unlinked by documents; Vallat notes a break before the Middle Elamite period but no mechanism. Britannica speculates Kassites may have caused a fall c.1600; Negahban (Iranica, Haft Tepe) calls 1505-1350 a dark period.

successor: Delhi Sultanate (Tughluq province of Ma'bar), later Madurai Sultanate
source2: Tansen Sen, 'The Yuan Khanate and India: Cross-cultural Diplomacy in the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Centuries', Asia Major 19 (2006) - http://www2.ihp.sinica.edu.tw/file/1445ZBWAkRi.pdf
notes: Succession war between Kulasekhara's sons (c.1310) opened the way to invasions from Delhi from 1311; Tughluq forces annexed Madurai as Ma'bar c.1323; Pandyas survived as minor rulers outside the core. Sen dates full northern Muslim control by 1333.
